about: Hand-built pairs, each one a case a naive matcher gets wrong, with the decision the resolver
reaches and the reason. These are NOT labels: nothing here enters the corpus, the evaluation or
any published metric. They are a regression suite for behaviours the aggregate cannot see,
because each of these shapes occurs a handful of times in 12,984 real pairs and breaking one
would move precision by 0.0002 and turn nothing red.
`expect` is one of match / review / no_match, and is the decision the shipped resolver makes.
A case expecting `review` is asserting that the resolver declines, which is a real answer here.
`known_limitation: true` marks a case where the recorded decision is NOT the one a person would
want. Those are kept, and kept visible, rather than deleted or quietly relabelled. The hold-out
was scored at commit b67b83e and ADR-001 fixes that no rule changes afterwards, so each of these
is a defect this build ships with and the next increment fixes -- which is a more useful thing
to publish than a suite engineered to be green.

cases.why: The same company written in two registries' conventions. Canonicalisation, not deletion.
`Sp. z o.o.` and its spelled-out form are one legal form; a token lookup never saw it.

right.legal_name: NORDIC CAPITAL SPOLKA Z OGRANICZONA ODPOWIEDZIALNOSCIA

cases.why: One system stored the accent and the other did not. This is the commonest drift in GLEIF.
The registrar's number is the fact. The names disagreeing does not get a vote.
One registrar, two numbers, two companies. The case the whole hard-signal order exists for.
Two SEC series, one product name. Exact name agreement used to win here and was wrong.
95% identical strings naming two products. A similarity average cannot see the year.
`I` against `II` is the entire identity of these two partnerships.

left.legal_name: Pan Ivy Growth Partners I LLC

right.legal_name: Pan Ivy Growth Partners II LLC

cases.why: 0.87 Jaro-Winkler from a long shared prefix. Distinctive-token weighting pulls it to 0.729 -- out of any merge band and into a person's queue, which is what that feature is for.

left.legal_name: Schindlers Reg. Treuunternehmen as Trustee of the Brahms Trust

right.legal_name: Schindlers Reg. Treuunternehmen as Trustee of the Clandeboye Trust

cases.why: A parenthesised code appended by one system; the same company. The discriminator rule correctly stops denying it (ADR-002), but nothing promotes it either: with THRESHOLD_MATCH None only a registrar's number or an exact name can assert a match, and neither is present. A person has to confirm it.

`P/L` is an abbreviation of `Pty Ltd` and splits into two single letters. The discriminator rule no longer denies the pair, but `p l` is not in the legal-form table, so the names never canonicalise to the same string and the pair stops at REVIEW. Adding the spelling is a rule change, and the hold-out is spent.
`&` is expanded rather than dropped, so `Smith & Nephew` reaches `Smith and Nephew`.

right.legal_name: SMITH AND NEPHEW PUBLIC LIMITED COMPANY

cases.why: Two registries issue the same digits to unrelated companies. Authority is half the key.
`Global Credit` against `International Bond`. Genuinely ambiguous; a person should look.
A merger or a rename, and nothing in the record says which. Declining is the answer.
Companies convert. Denying on the legal form alone cost 76 adjudicated duplicates (ADR-002).

The resolver gets this wrong. `acronym_match` carries 0.04 of the weight -- argued from meaning before any result existed -- and 0.04 cannot lift a pair whose strings share almost nothing to 0.66. It scores 0.389 and is denied. Raising that weight is a rule change against a spent hold-out, so it is published as a miss instead.
`Holdings` is not evidence. Without the frequency table it would look like overlap.
